https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: ‘Principled’ vandals must be made to pay
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
The woman who sprayed with red paint and then repeatedly slashed a portrait of Lord Balfour at Trinity College, Cambridge, last weekend has not been identified. She appeared to be wearing a Mulberry backpack (marketed by the brand as “the ultimate in practical ladies’ luxury”) but that is all the police have to go on. Well, they do know the organisation responsible: a group called Palestine Action issued a press release (“images and videos are available for free here”) boasting that it had “ruined a 1914 painting by Philip Alexius de Laszlo … [of] the colonial administrator and signatory of the Balfour declaration”.
This was the pledge later made by that British prime minister to support a “national home for the Jewish people” in the Ottoman territory of Palestine. The press release from Palestine Action declared it would continue its campaign of direct action “until … British complicity with the colonisation of Palestine ends”. Or, in other words, until the British government agrees Israel should cease to exist.
In the meantime who should pay for the repair of the portrait? If it is indeed “ruined” as Palestine Action claims, that would be quite a bill. Portraits by de Laszlo, a Hungarian Jew who settled in this country in 1907, can sell for tens of thousands of pounds. I bet it will be Trinity College that foots the bill — or its insurer. But it should be Palestine Action or, if she can be apprehended, its Mulberry-toting slasher-in-residence.
One of the oddities in how such crimes of allegedly principled vandalism are dealt with is that the perpetrators are not faced with the full costs of their actions, even if convicted. In cases where the value of the damage is “less than £5,000”, the maximum fine is “up to £2,500”. Why not up to £4,999?
This issue has much wider application than in the area of fine-art destruction (a particular favourite of the Just Stop Oil campaign, an offshoot of Extinction Rebellion). In November, the week after members of this group had attacked Velázquez’s Rokeby Venus in the National Gallery, I observed that the co-founder of Extinction Rebellion Gail Bradbrook “will never have to pay the £27,500 replacement cost of the large pane of reinforced security glass at the Department of Transport” that she smashed with a hammer, even though the court had rejected “her argument that she ‘had permission from nature’ to demolish it”.
And I suggested (noting that these “direct action” groups are funded to the extent of many millions of pounds by the Climate Emergency Fund in the US), “Perhaps the law should treat such organisations as it does football clubs: with some proportion of financial responsibility for the policing costs they impose on the public.”
It turns out I am not the only one thinking along these lines. Much more importantly, so is Lord Walney, formerly the Labour MP John Woodcock, who as a crossbench peer is the government’s independent adviser on political violence and disruption. Walney was commissioned to produce proposals on how our handling of such matters could be improved, not least in terms of policing. His report, “Protecting Our Democracy from Coercion”, is to be presented to the prime minister later this month.
A draft I have seen makes the point that the continual “Palestine” demonstrations over the past five months have already cost the police — or rather us — as much as £20 million: “When groups run so many mass protests, the authorities should consider whether organisers should be asked to contribute to policing costs … There is something of a precedent here … In 2019 the police were able to claim back £5.5 million out of a total of £48 million for policing football matches.”
Apparently this suggestion is meeting resistance within the bureaucracy, not just on grounds of protecting “freedom of assembly” but, more practically, because protest groups can be chameleon-like in changing from one identity to another (as with the various offshoots of Extinction Rebellion).Walney has another go in an amended draft, noting that because “the frontline resources of the Metropolitan police … stand to be seriously depleted by the spiralling costs of policing the Gaza marches [and] the system cannot run on cancelling rest days and overtime in perpetuity without a significant detrimental effect on frontline policing”, the Met should be able to use a “resources” argument to limit the number of marches. It isn’t yet possible for the Met to do that, it seems: a change in the law would be required.
That would make sense even to those who do not feel remotely threatened by the constant Gaza demonstrations. In the wake of the two immensely disruptive Extinction Rebellion “events” in London in 2019, a report by HM Inspector of Constabulary revealed that the “policing operation for the two extended protests cost £37 million, more than twice the annual budget of London’s violent crime task force”.
Puzzlingly, the one time the police did apply financial arguments to such matters was when, as Walney records: “In 2015 the Metropolitan police told the Passion for Freedom art exhibition that it would have to pay £36,000 towards policing costs if an exhibit by the artist Mimsy was included, as it mocked Islamic State.” This was justified on the grounds of public protection, but, as one art critic wrote at the time, “To let fear of bigots and maniacs rule our art galleries is a betrayal of the civilisation we claim to uphold.”
Anyway, it is time that those who would disrupt the lives of millions, in a futile attempt to bend the elected government to their will, are pursued for at least some of the financial costs, if possible by those whose businesses have suffered. A meeting of a hundred or so Just Stop Oil members this month was told by the group’s co-founder Indigo Rumbelow that its next campaign would involve activity at the country’s airports during the summer holiday peak: “The plan … could involve disrupting people on their holidays … it’s not comfortable to disrupt ordinary people but it’s completely necessary.” Or, as JSO declared, vaingloriously, after what transpired at the meeting was revealed by an undercover reporter: “This summer we will take action at airports to create enormous disruption.”
A particular problem for distressed travellers is — if the campaign is not thwarted by the police — that airlines are not responsible for reimbursing passengers for cancelled flights or hotel bookings foregone if the disruption is not their fault. The holidaymakers are completely stuffed, just for being, in Ms Rumbelow’s words, “ordinary people”.
The Just Stop Oil lot are fond of saying that “the polluter must pay”. Actually, we need to make the fanatics fork out.
